The following subsections discuss these three areas, infrastructure needs, operational implications, and emissions controls and efficiency, to highlight how non-drop-in fuels may influence both costs and day-to-day performance in the freight rail sector. Infrastructure Needs Non-drop-in fuels impose additional infrastructure requirements that extend beyond a simple substitution for conventional diesel. One of the main considerations is fuel storage and handling. Because fuels such as methanol and ethanol have lower energy densities, they require significantly larger storage volumes to deliver the same energy output, which affects the design and capacity of both onboard locomotive tanks and refueling depots. In addition, some of these fuels have chemical properties that demand specialized materials and enhanced safety measures to prevent leaks and ensure compatibility with storage systems. Meeting these needs often translates into additional capital expenditure, either for retrofitting existing facilities or building new infrastructure. Refueling infrastructure also presents challenges. Establishing a reliable supply chain for non-drop-in fuels requires new distribution networks and strategically located refueling stations, which can be costly and time-consuming to implement. Moreover, the use of specialized equipment and procedures can lengthen refueling times, potentially disrupting train schedules and reducing overall operational efficiency. Operational Implications Beyond infrastructure, the adoption of non-drop-in fuels carries operational implications for locomotives themselves. These impacts relate to the extent of retrofitting required, as well as potential effects on maintenance and reliability: • Retrofitting Requirements: Non-drop-in fuels often necessitate significant engine modifications to ensure compatibility and optimal performance. These modifications can include changes to fuel injection systems, combustion chambers, and emissions control technologies. • Maintenance and Reliability: The use of alternative fuels can affect engine wear and maintenance schedules. For instance, BD’s solvent properties may lead to increased filter clogging, requiring more frequent maintenance and potentially impacting reliability. 31 Emissions Controls and Efficiency The use of alternative fuels also has implications for emissions control technologies and overall efficiency. In some cases, these adjustments are necessary to maintain compliance with air quality standards: • Additional Emissions Equipment: Certain fuels may produce higher levels of specific emissions, necessitating enhanced emissions control systems. For example, fuels with higher NO emissions might require selective catalytic reduction systems, which use urea X as a reducing agent. • Efficiency Considerations: The integration of additional emissions controls and the use of less energy-dense fuels can place an efficiency burden on train operations.
